standard_text: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context in multiple ways, such as: a. Report the number of observations; b. Describe the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement; c. Determine quantitative measures of center (mean and/or median) and spread (range and interquartile range); d. Describe any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered; and e. Relate the choice of measures of center and spread to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.

progression.narrative: 6.DS.3 asks students to summarize a numerical data set in context: report how many observations there are, name the attribute and its units, find measures of center (mean and median) and spread (range and interquartile range), and describe the shape, clusters, peaks, gaps, and outliers. The on-grade work moves from finding the median, mode, and range and computing the mean, to reading real displays and reporting observations, then to the interquartile range from a box plot, and finally to letting the shape decide which center to trust. Students who struggle here usually carry gaps from well below grade six, most often shaky whole-number division and multi-digit addition and subtraction, which stall every mean and every range. One grade below, the grade five work of building and reading a line plot and finding the mean, median, and range of a whole-number set is the bridge that must be solid first. Intervention should rebuild the arithmetic, then the grade five statistics, and only then return to summarizing data in context.

steps.rationale: Part (c) names the median and range first because they only require ordering -- and ordering-before-middle is the habit every later measure leans on.
The mean is part (c)'s other center. It gets its own step because its procedure (add all, divide) must be welded to its NAME before mean and median stop swapping in students' heads.
Parts (a) and (b): every summary starts by counting the observations and naming the attribute and units -- reading the display before computing from it.
Part (c)'s deeper spread measure: the IQR from a box plot, where Indiana's exclude-the-median quartile convention lives.
Parts (d) and (e): clusters, peaks, gaps, and outliers -- and the judgment call the shape forces: which measure of center to trust.
The standard's ceiling: reasoning about how each measure responds when the data changes -- the bridge to grade 7's comparisons of data sets.

skills.name: Add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers

prerequisite_skill.description: Add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers by lining up place values and regrouping.

skills.i_do_script: Adding and subtracting is really about matching place values: ones with ones, tens with tens. Watch me add 128 + 47. I stack them so the ones line up under the ones. Ones: 8 + 7 = 15, so I write 5 and carry 1 ten. Tens: 2 + 4 + 1 = 7. Hundreds: 1. The sum is 175. For 52 - 8, I cannot take 8 from 2, so I regroup a ten into ten ones: now 12 - 8 = 4 ones and 4 tens are left, giving 44. Line up the places, then work one column at a time.

canonical_error.pattern: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in a column instead of regrouping
canonical_error.example: For 52 - 8 the student does 8 - 2 in the ones place and writes 56 instead of 44
canonical_error.why: You cannot take 8 from 2, so a ten must be regrouped into ten ones. Flipping the digits changes the value, but regrouping keeps it true.

skills.item_template: Two multi-digit whole numbers to add or subtract, clean regrouping, no calculator. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for forgetting to carry the ten
Watch for doing 8 - 2 instead of regrouping
Watch for forgetting to carry the ten
Watch for subtracting each digit the wrong way
Watch for carrying into the wrong column
Watch for trouble regrouping across the zeros
Watch for forgetting to carry into the hundreds
Watch for regrouping the wrong place

redirect_script.stop: Wait, are your ones lined up under your ones?
redirect_script.prompt: Stack the numbers so each place sits over its match, then work one column at a time. If you cannot subtract, regroup a ten before you take away.
redirect_script.praise: You lined up the places and regrouped, so every digit landed where it belongs.

vocabulary.definition: Trade ten of one place for one of the next larger place, or the reverse, so you can add or subtract.
The size a digit has because of its position: ones, tens, hundreds.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 addition and subtraction within 1000 using base-ten blocks before retrying.

worked_example_script.text: Write 128 + 47 stacked, ones under ones, and draw place-value columns labeled hundreds, tens, ones.
Add the ones: 8 + 7. Is that more than 9? What do we do with the extra ten?
8 + 7 = 15, so write 5 and carry 1 ten. Tens: 2 + 4 + 1 = 7. Hundreds: 1. The sum is 175.
If a student writes 56 for 52 - 8, hand them base-ten blocks: can you take 8 ones from 2 ones without trading a ten?
Your turn: line up and solve 63 + 29.

skills.name: Divide a whole number into equal groups

prerequisite_skill.description: Divide within 100 to share a total into equal groups with no remainder.

skills.i_do_script: Dividing is sharing a total into equal groups. Watch me share 24 among 4: I deal them out one to each group until they are gone, and each group ends with 6, so 24 divided by 4 is 6. I can also picture 24 counters in an array of 4 equal rows, and each row is 6. The answer is the size of one equal group. That equal-share number is exactly the number the mean will land on when I share a data total evenly.

canonical_error.pattern: Subtracts the number of groups from the total instead of dividing
canonical_error.example: For share 30 among 5 the student answers 25 (30 - 5) instead of 6
canonical_error.why: The student grabs the nearest operation instead of sharing. Splitting a total into equal groups is division, and each group must end up the same size.

skills.item_template: A total shared equally among a number of groups, facts within 100, no remainders, no calculator. Short response fluency bank.

skills.name: Represent and read a numerical data set on a line plot

prerequisite_skill.description: Show a data set as X's on a line plot and read the total number of data points from it.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A line plot has 2 X's over 3 and 1 X over 5. How many data points are shown?

skills.i_do_script: A line plot puts one X over each value on a number line, so every X stands for one data point. Watch me read this plot: 3 X's over 6, 1 X over 7, and 2 X's over 9. To count the observations I add the X's, not the number of stacks: 3 + 1 + 2 = 6 data points. The value that appears most often is the tallest stack, here 6. To build a plot from a list like 5, 6, 6, 8, 6, I put an X over each number as I read it, so 6 gets 3 X's.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts the number of different values on the line plot instead of the total number of X's
canonical_error.example: A plot has X's over three values, so the student says there are 3 observations instead of adding the X's to get 6
canonical_error.why: Each X is one observation. The number of observations is the total count of X's across all the stacks, not how many different numbers happen to have an X.

skills.item_template: A small line plot described by its stacks (how many X's over each value), or a short data list to plot. Student counts observations, reads a frequency, or names the most common value. Numeric or short response.

A line plot has 1 X over 2, 2 X's over 3, and 2 X's over 5. How many observations are there?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 is the number of different values (the canonical error); 2 is the tallest single stack; 10 is doubling the count

sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 and 6 each have only 2 X's; 8 is the total number of X's, not a value

redirect_script.stop: Wait, are you counting stacks or X's?

redirect_script.praise: You added every X, so your count of observations is trustworthy.

vocabulary.definition: A number line with an X above each value to show how often that value occurs.
One data point, shown by one X on a line plot.

skills.name: Find the mean, median, and range of a whole-number data set

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the mean, median, mode, and range of a small set of whole numbers.

skills.i_do_script: These four measures each answer one question. Watch me with 2, 4, 9. The mean is the fair share: add every value, 2 + 4 + 9 = 15, then divide by how many, 15 divided by 3 = 5. The median is the middle after ordering: 2, 4, 9, so the median is 4. The mode is the value that shows up most, and here every value appears once, so there is no mode. The range is greatest minus least: 9 - 2 = 7. Add and divide for the mean, order and find the middle for the median.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the values but forgets to divide, reporting the total as the mean
canonical_error.example: For 2, 4, 9 the student says the mean is 15 instead of 5
canonical_error.why: The student stops after the adding step. The mean is the fair-share amount, so the total must still be split equally among the number of values.

skills.item_template: A small whole-number data set. Student finds the mean (clean division, no remainder), the median, the mode, or the range. Numeric or short response, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: Find the mean of 3, 7, 8, 2.
Find the median of 8, 3, 9, 5, 7.
Find the range of 4, 9, 6, 2.
Find the mode of 5, 8, 5, 2, 5, 9.
Find the mean of 10, 12, 8.
Find the median of 12, 4, 9.
Find the median of these quiz scores: 6, 2, 9, 4, 8.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9 is the middle of the unordered list (order-first error); 7 is the range; 5.8 is the mean

sample_items.stem: Find the mean of these ages: 2, 4, 9.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 is the median; 7 is the range; 15 is the total (forgot to divide by 3)

redirect_script.stop: Wait, is that the mean or just the total?
redirect_script.prompt: The mean is a fair share, so after you add every value you still divide by how many values there are. Order first before you hunt for a median.
redirect_script.praise: You added and then divided, so that fair-share number really is the mean.

vocabulary.definition: Add all the values, then divide by how many; the fair-share amount.
The middle value after the data is ordered least to greatest.
Greatest value minus least value; how far the data spreads.

worked_example_script.text: Write the data 2, 4, 9 and set out counters: 2, then 4, then 9 in three piles.
For the mean, what do we do first, and what must we still do after we add?
Add every value: 2 + 4 + 9 = 15. Then share it equally among the 3 values: 15 divided by 3 = 5, so the mean is 5.
If a student says 15, push the counters into 3 equal piles and ask how many are in one pile.
Your turn: order 2, 4, 9 and give the median, then find the range.

skills.name: Determine the median, mode, and range of a data set

prerequisite_skill.description: Order a set of numbers and identify least, greatest, and middle values
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Order 9, 4, 7 from least to greatest. Which number is in the middle?
prerequisite_skill.if_student_says: If they say 4 (the middle of the list as written), they are not ordering first -- start at Foundation skill F1 before this one.

skills.i_do_script: Watch me find the median of 8, 3, 9, 5, 7. Before I touch the word 'median,' I order the list: 3, 5, 7, 8, 9. Now I cover one number from each end at the same time -- one from the left, one from the right -- until one number is left standing in the middle: 7. That's the median. The range is greatest minus least: 9 - 3 = 6. The mode is the value that shows up most often -- here every value appears once, so this set has no mode.

canonical_error.pattern: Finds the 'middle' of the list as it is written instead of ordering the data first
canonical_error.example: For 14, 8, 20, 11, 6, the student points at 20 (the middle value as written) and calls it the median instead of ordering to 6, 8, 11, 14, 20 and finding 11
canonical_error.why: The student memorized 'median = middle number' as a position rule and applies it to the raw list. They don't understand the median is the middle of the VALUES, which only lands in the middle position after the data is ordered.

redirect_script.stop: Freeze -- did you put the numbers in order first?
redirect_script.prompt: Rewrite the whole list from least to greatest before you look for the middle. Then cover one number from each end at the same time until one is left. Is your middle number the same one you had before?
redirect_script.praise: You ordered first, then found the middle -- that's exactly how the median works every time.

skills.item_template: An unordered list of 5-7 whole-number data values with a real-world context. Student finds the median, mode, or range. MC with 4 choices; distractors are the unordered middle, the mean, the range, or the maximum.

sample_items.stem: Find the median of these quiz scores: 8, 3, 9, 5, 7.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9 is the middle of the UNORDERED list (the canonical error); 6 is the range; 6.4 is the mean

sample_items.stem: Find the mode of these points scored per game: 12, 15, 11, 15, 9, 14, 15.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 14 is the median; 6 is the range; 9 is the minimum

sample_items.stem: Find the median of this data set: 4, 9, 2, 7, 5, 9.
sample_items.distractor_logic: An even count means averaging the two middle values; 7 and 5 each take only one middle value; 9 is the mode

sample_items.stem: Find the range of these ages of club members: 16, 11, 20, 11, 13.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 20 is just the maximum (forgot to subtract); 13 is the median; 11 is the mode

vocabulary.definition: The middle value AFTER the data is ordered least to greatest. With an even count, average the two middle values.
The value that appears most often. A set can have no mode or more than one.
Greatest value minus least value -- one number that tells how spread out the data is.
A single number, like the median or mean, that describes where the middle of the data sits.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to 6DS3-S2: the other measure of center, the mean -- add them all and share equally.
next_steps.if_fail: Check Foundation skill F1 (ordering). If ordering is solid, re-run S1 with 5-value sets and the cover-from-both-ends move.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Quiz scores: 8, 3, 9, 5, 7. Find the median.'
Before we hunt for the middle -- is this list in order? How can you tell?
Order it least to greatest for me. What do you get?
Count their ordered list -- it must still have 5 values. A dropped value here poisons the median.
Write the ordered list 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 and cover the two end numbers with your fingers.
Keep covering one from each end at the same time. What number is left standing alone?
So the median is 7. Quick contrast: if I had just grabbed the middle of the original messy list, what would I have gotten, and why is that wrong?
Order first, THEN middle. The median is the middle of the values, not the middle of wherever the numbers happened to land on the page.

materials: One printed problem card per group

1. Show the group Ava's work and let them react before you say anything.

content.error_step: Ava took the middle of the list as written instead of ordering the data first.
content.why: The median is the middle of the ordered values. Sorted, the data is 6, 8, 11, 14, 20, and the middle value is 11.

activities.title: Human Number Line Median
materials: Index cards with one data value each
activities.instructions:
1. Hand each of 5-7 students a card with a data value and have them stand in random order.
2. Ask the class: can we find the median right now? Why not?
3. Have the card-holders sort themselves least to greatest.
4. Pair off students from the two ends and have the pairs sit down together until one student (or two) remains standing -- that's the median (or average the two).
5. Debrief: what did we have to do BEFORE the pairing-off trick worked?

activities.title: Which Measure Is It?
activities.instructions:
1. Partners match each description card to its measure card.
2. Both partners must agree before a match locks in.
3. Debrief with the decoy: 'the middle number of the list as written' matches NOTHING -- ask why.

pairs.left: The value that appears most often
Add all values, divide by how many

decoys: The middle number of the list as written

strategy_links.why: Analyzing an unordered-median mistake surfaces the 'order first' rule better than being told it.
Physically sorting cards or classmates (concrete) before doing it on paper (abstract) anchors why ordering comes first.
Whiteboard Pass makes every student's ordered list visible, so dropped values get caught immediately.

questioning_prompts: Is the data in order yet? How do you know?
How many values are in the original list, and how many are in your ordered list?
Is the count odd or even? What does that tell you about how the middle will work?
Which is the median measuring -- the middle POSITION on the page, or the middle of the VALUES?
Could the range be bigger than the greatest value? Why not?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student points at the middle number of the unordered list and calls it the median.
misconception_redirects.say: Rewrite the whole list from least to greatest before you look for the middle. Then cover one number from each end at the same time until one is left. Is your middle number the same one you had before?
misconception_redirects.praise: You ordered first, then found the middle -- that's exactly how the median works every time.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reports the greatest value as the range instead of subtracting the least.
misconception_redirects.say: The range is a DISTANCE, not a place. Underline the greatest value and the least value, then subtract to find how far apart they are.
misconception_redirects.praise: Greatest minus least -- now your range tells how spread out the data really is.

steps.annotation: The median hides in the ORDERED list -- always order first.

steps.math: Cross off ends in pairs: 3 & 9, then the next pair
steps.annotation: Removing one value from each end at the same time keeps the middle balanced.
One value is left standing -- that's the median.
Range is greatest minus least: how wide the data stretches.

faded_example.stem: Find the median and range of: 10, 4, 12, 7, 9.

steps.annotation: The ordering step is done for you.
Cross off one value from each end at a time. Which value is left in the middle?
Now subtract: greatest minus least gives the range.

The range is ___ minus ___, which equals ___.

skills.name: Calculate the mean of a data set
skills.i_do_script: The mean levels everything out. Watch me with 20, 24, 19, 25: first I add every value -- 20 + 24 + 19 + 25 = 88. Then I share that total equally among the 4 values: 88 / 4 = 22. Two steps, always in this order: add them all, divide by how many. The mean is NOT the middle number -- that's the median's job.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps mean and median -- asked for the mean, the student orders the data and reports the middle value
canonical_error.example: Asked for the mean of 4, 6, 13, 9, 3, the student orders it and answers 6 (the median) instead of computing 35 / 5 = 7
canonical_error.why: Both measures answer 'what's typical?', so students treat the names as interchangeable. They latch onto whichever procedure feels easier (finding the middle) and haven't attached each NAME to its own PROCEDURE: median = middle of ordered list, mean = add all and divide.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- which measure did the question ask for?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the word 'mean' in the problem. Mean means add-them-all-then-divide-by-how-many. Finding the middle is the MEDIAN. Add the values out loud, then divide by the count.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the name to the right procedure -- add all, divide by the count. That's the mean.

vocabulary.definition: Add every value, then divide by how many values there are -- the fair-share or level-out number.
The total you get when you add all the values.
The MIDDLE value of the ordered list -- a different measure of center than the mean.

next_steps.if_fail: Check Foundation skill F2 (fair-share division). If dividing is solid, drill the two-step chant 'add them all, divide by how many' with 3-value sets.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'Laps swum this week: 20, 24, 19, 25. Find the mean.'
First -- does the question say mean or median? What's the difference in what we DO?
Step one for the mean: what do we do with all four numbers?
Write the sum: 20 + 24 + 19 + 25 = 88.
Step two: we share 88 equally. How many values did it come from, so what do we divide by?
If the student divides by a different number than the count of values, have them touch each data value and count aloud.
So the mean is 22. If every swim day had been exactly the same, how many laps would each day have been?
That's what the mean IS: the level-out number. Add them all, divide by how many -- every single time.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus was asked for the MEAN of a data set. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: The middle number is 6, so the mean is 6.
practice_problems.answer: Marcus found the MEDIAN, not the mean. Mean = (4 + 6 + 13 + 9 + 3) / 5 = 35 / 5 = 7.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical mean-vs-median swap. Marcus's arithmetic is flawless -- he answered the wrong question.

practice_problems.stem: Find the mean of: 1.5, 2.5, 2, 4.

practice_problems.stem: The mean of 5 values is 12. Four of the values are 10, 11, 13, 14. What is the fifth value?
practice_problems.answer: 12. The five values must total 5 x 12 = 60, and 10, 11, 13, 14 total 48, so the fifth is 60 - 48 = 12.
practice_problems.notes: Reverses direction: from the mean back to the data.

practice_problems.stem: Create a data set of 4 different whole numbers with a mean of 10.

activities.title: Marcus Answered the Wrong Question
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Marcus's work. Point out that every step he wrote is correct arithmetic.
2. Ask: so what went wrong? (He ran the MEDIAN procedure when the question asked for the MEAN.)
3. Have the group compute the actual mean.
4. Debrief: each student states one way to remember which name goes with which procedure.

content.worked_problem: Question: find the MEAN of 4, 6, 13, 9, 3. Marcus writes: 'Ordered: 3, 4, 6, 9, 13. The middle number is 6, so the mean is 6.'
content.error_step: Marcus ordered the data and took the middle value -- that procedure computes the median, not the mean.
content.why: Mean = add all and divide by the count: 35 / 5 = 7. The two measures of center have different procedures, and here they give different numbers.

activities.title: Level the Towers
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair builds towers matching a data set, e.g. 3, 5, 4, 8, 5 (one tower per value).
2. Challenge: move cubes between towers until every tower is the same height. No cubes may be added or removed.
3. Ask: what height did every tower become? (5 -- the mean.)
4. Then compute 25 / 5 on paper and connect: adding all = counting every cube; dividing = leveling.
5. Debrief: why does moving cubes never change the total?

activities.title: Mean or Median? Name the Procedure
activities.instructions:
1. Lay two headers: MEAN and MEDIAN.
2. Partners sort each card under the measure it belongs to.
3. Challenge round: both partners must justify the two 'trap' cards (the ones that mention 'middle' and 'typical').
4. Debrief: which cards were hardest and why?

cards.text: Order the data first, then find the middle
Cross off one value from each end
With an even count, average the two middle values

strategy_links.why: Leveling cube towers (concrete) gives the mean a physical meaning before the add-and-divide procedure (abstract).
Pairing a correct mean computation with Marcus's median-swap error makes the name-to-procedure link explicit.
Number Talks on 'what must the total be?' build the sum-then-share reasoning the mean depends on.

questioning_prompts: Does the question say mean or median? What procedure goes with that name?
What is the total of all the values? What do we divide it by, and why that number?
If every value were leveled out to be equal, what would each one be?
Can the mean be a number that isn't in the data set? Why?
Your answer is bigger than the largest data value -- can that ever happen for a mean?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Asked for the mean, the student orders the list and reports the middle value.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the word 'mean' in the problem. Mean means add-them-all-then-divide-by-how-many. Finding the middle is the MEDIAN. Add the values out loud, then divide by the count.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the name to the right procedure -- add all, divide by the count. That's the mean.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds correctly but divides by the wrong number (e.g. divides a 5-value sum by 4).
misconception_redirects.say: Touch each data value and count them aloud. The divisor is exactly how many values you just touched -- not one more, not one less.
misconception_redirects.praise: You counted the values and divided by exactly that many -- that's the fair share.

quick_checks.look_for: 6, via 18 / 3. Right answer with no sum shown may be the median shortcut -- ask 'what was the total?' to check they ran the mean procedure.

steps.annotation: Step 1: add every value to get the total.
The divisor is how many data values there are.
Step 2: share the total equally -- that's the mean, the level-out number.
The total is done for you.
How many values are in the data set?
Divide the total by the count to finish the mean.

skills.name: Report observations and describe the attribute and units of a data display
skills.i_do_script: Before we compute anything, we read the display like a story. Watch me with a dot plot of books read: each dot is ONE student -- one observation. I count the dots, not the numbers under the line: 8 dots means 8 students. Then I ask, what was measured? Books read. In what units? Books -- a count. Number observed, what was measured, and its units: that's the summary every data set starts with.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts the axis labels or reads the largest axis number instead of counting the dots to find the number of observations
canonical_error.example: A dot plot with 9 dots on an axis labeled 2 through 6 -- the student answers '5 observations' (five axis numbers) or '6' (the biggest label) instead of 9
canonical_error.why: The student doesn't yet see that each dot IS one piece of data. They treat the printed numbers as the data because numbers feel like data, while the dots look like decoration.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- what does one dot stand for?
redirect_script.prompt: Touch each dot and count out loud, column by column. The numbers under the line are ADDRESSES where dots live -- the dots themselves are the data.
redirect_script.praise: You counted every dot -- each one is one observation, and now your count matches the real data set.

skills.name: Determine the interquartile range from a box plot or data set
skills.i_do_script: A box plot squeezes a whole data set into five numbers. Watch me read this one: the whiskers end at 10 and 26 -- the minimum and maximum. The BOX runs from Q1 = 14 to Q3 = 22, and the line inside it is the median, 18. The interquartile range is the width of the box: Q3 - Q1 = 22 - 14 = 8. That's the spread of the MIDDLE HALF of the data -- not the whole stretch from end to end.

canonical_error.pattern: Computes max minus min (the range) when asked for the IQR
canonical_error.example: For a box plot with whiskers at 3 and 15 and box edges at 5 and 12, the student answers 12 (15 - 3) instead of Q3 - Q1 = 7
canonical_error.why: Both measures are 'big number minus small number,' so the student grabs the most visible endpoints -- the whisker tips. They haven't attached the IQR to the BOX (the middle 50%), so the whole plot's ends feel like the right numbers to use.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- did you use the box or the whiskers?
redirect_script.prompt: Put one finger on each EDGE of the box. Those are Q1 and Q3. The IQR is the distance between your fingers -- subtract the left edge from the right edge. The whisker tips give the range, a different measure.
redirect_script.praise: You subtracted the box edges -- Q3 minus Q1. That's the IQR, the spread of the middle half.

skills.name: Describe distribution shape and choose measures using outliers
skills.i_do_script: Watch me read the SHAPE of this dot plot of bus waits: 11, 12, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 30. Most dots cluster from 11 to 15 -- that's the cluster, with a peak at the tallest stack. Then one dot sits way out at 30 after a big gap: an outlier. Here's the punchline: the mean is 15 but the median is 13. The outlier dragged the mean up -- the mean has to absorb every value. The median just counts to the middle, so 30 barely matters to it. Outlier in the data? Trust the median.

canonical_error.pattern: Believes the outlier affects the median more than the mean (swaps which measure is resistant)
canonical_error.example: For 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 40, the student claims the outlier 40 'makes the median huge' -- but the median is 10 with or without 40, while the mean falls from about 14.29 to 10 when 40 is removed
canonical_error.why: The student knows 'the outlier messes up one of them' but hasn't connected WHY: the mean is computed FROM every value, so an extreme value pours straight into the sum; the median is found by position, so one far-away value only shifts the line-up by one spot.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- test that claim with the actual numbers.
redirect_script.prompt: Compute the median with the outlier, then cross the outlier off and compute it again. Now do the same for the mean. Which one actually moved?
redirect_script.praise: You tested it -- the mean moved and the median held still. Outliers pour into the sum, not the middle.

Neither measure changes when a value is removed.

practice_problems.stem: The data set 4, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 25 has a mean of 9 and a median of 7. Which measure better describes a typical value, and why?

practice_problems.stem: A dot plot of test scores shows dots from 70 to 85, then nothing until a single dot at 100. Name the feature at 100 and one feature the 70-85 dots form.

skills.name: Predict how center and spread change when data is added
skills.i_do_script: Now we predict BEFORE we compute. Scores 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 have a mean of 12. A new score of 30 is coming in. My prediction move: compare the new value to the CURRENT mean. 30 is way above 12, so the mean must rise. Check: new sum 90, divided by 6 values = 15. The median only slides one position -- from 12 to 13. One rule runs this whole skill: above the mean pulls it up, below the mean pulls it down, equal to the mean leaves it alone.

canonical_error.pattern: Believes adding any new value must increase the mean because the data set got bigger
canonical_error.example: For 15, 18, 21 (mean 18), the student predicts that adding 12 raises the mean -- but 12 is below 18, so the mean drops to 16.5
canonical_error.why: The student conflates 'more data' with 'more total.' They ignore that the divisor grows too: a new value only raises the mean if it's bigger than the current mean, because the mean is a balance point, not a running total.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- compare the new value to the mean first.
redirect_script.prompt: Write the current mean. Is the new value above it, below it, or equal to it? Above pulls the mean up, below pulls it down, equal leaves it alone. Now compute and check your prediction.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the new value to the mean before predicting -- that's the balance-point thinking.

skills.item_template: A data set of 3-6 values with a new value being added. Student predicts and/or computes how the mean, median, or range changes -- or finds the value needed to hit a target mean. MC or two-part response.

sample_items.stem: A student's game scores are 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 (mean 12, median 12). A new score of 30 is added. What happens to the mean and the median?
sample_items.answer: The mean rises to 15; the median rises only to 13.
choices: The mean rises to 15; the median rises only to 13.
Both stay at 12 because one score can't change a whole data set.
The median jumps to 15; the mean moves only to 13.
Only the range changes; the mean and median never change when data is added.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Swapping the mean's and median's movements is the S5 canonical error resurfacing; the other choices deny that a new value shifts the sum and the middle.

sample_items.stem: The data set 5, 7, 9 has a mean of 7. A new value of 7 -- exactly the mean -- is added. What happens to the mean?
sample_items.answer: It stays at 7: adding a value equal to the mean doesn't tip the balance.
choices: It stays at 7: adding a value equal to the mean doesn't tip the balance.
It increases, because adding any value increases the mean.
It decreases, because there are more values to divide by.
It doubles, because the data set got bigger.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Adding any value increases the mean' is the canonical error; 'more values to divide by' forgets the sum grew too; doubling invents a rule.

sample_items.stem: Daily temperatures were 20, 22, 24, 26 (mean 23). A cold day of 8 degrees is added. What happens to the mean?
sample_items.answer: It drops to 20, because 8 is far below the old mean.
choices: It drops to 20, because 8 is far below the old mean.
It rises above 23, because adding a value always raises the mean.
It stays 23, because the middle two values didn't change.
It becomes 8, the newest value.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Always raises' is the canonical error; 'middle didn't change' confuses mean with median; 'becomes 8' treats the newest value as the summary.

sample_items.stem: A gymnast's scores are 10, 12, 14. What fourth score would make the mean of all four scores exactly 13?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 13 assumes the new value must equal the target mean; 12 averages the existing values; 52 is the needed TOTAL (4 x 13), not the missing value. Needed: 52 - 36 = 16.

vocabulary.definition: The mean acts like a see-saw balance: values above it pull it up, values below pull it down.
The three possible effects on a measure when a value is added -- always name which one and why.
A mean you want the data to have; work backward from total = mean x count to find the missing value.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.DSP.2-style work: comparing two data sets using their measures of center and spread.
next_steps.if_fail: Return to 6DS3-S2's leveling model, then re-run predictions with 3-value sets where the student computes both before and after every time.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'Scores: 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. Mean 12, median 12. A new score of 30 comes in.'
Before any arithmetic: is 30 above or below the current mean of 12? So which way should the mean move?
Will the mean move a little or a lot? What about the new value makes you say that?
Compute together: new sum = 90, new count = 6, new mean = 15.
Now the median. Write the new ordered list 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 30. Where's the middle now, and what is it?
If the student expects the median to jump like the mean did, have them compare: mean moved 3 points, median moved 1. Ask why the difference.
And the range -- did the new value land outside the old min and max? So what's the new range?
The prediction rule: compare the new value to the current mean. Above pulls up, below pulls down, equal changes nothing. Then verify with the two-step mean.

practice_problems.stem: The data 5, 7, 9 has mean 7. Without computing, will adding a 10 raise or lower the mean?
practice_problems.answer: Raise it -- 10 is above the current mean, so it pulls the balance point up.

practice_problems.stem: Can adding a new value ever make the range SMALLER? Why or why not?
practice_problems.answer: No. The new value either lands inside the old min-max (range unchanged) or outside it (range grows).

practice_problems.stem: Scores: 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. Add 30. Compute the new mean and new median.
Temperatures: 20, 22, 24, 26. A day of 8 degrees is added. Compute the new mean and new range.
Noah predicted what a new data value would do. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: A new value of 12 is added.
Adding a value makes the data set bigger, so the mean must increase.
practice_problems.answer: Adding a value only raises the mean if the value is ABOVE the old mean. 12 is below 18, so the mean falls: (12 + 15 + 18 + 21) / 4 = 16.5.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical 'adding any value increases the mean' error.

practice_problems.stem: Data: 5, 7, 9. Add a 7. What happens to the mean and the median?
practice_problems.answer: Nothing -- both stay at 7. A value equal to the mean (and middle) doesn't tip either measure.

practice_problems.stem: The mean of 10, 12, 14 is 12. Find a fourth value that makes the mean 13, and explain your method.
practice_problems.answer: 16. Four values with mean 13 must total 4 x 13 = 52; the current total is 36, so the new value is 52 - 36 = 16.

practice_problems.stem: Create a data set of 4 values, then add a fifth value that raises the mean but does NOT change the median.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 2, 8, 8, 10 (mean 7, median 8). Add 22: the ordered set is 2, 8, 8, 10, 22, so the median is still 8 but the mean rises to 50 / 5 = 10. Full credit for any set where the student verifies both measures before and after.

activities.title: Does Bigger Data Mean a Bigger Mean?
activities.instructions:
1. Show Noah's claim: 'adding a value makes the data set bigger, so the mean must increase.'
2. Ask the group to vote agree/disagree BEFORE computing.
3. Compute the new mean together: (15 + 18 + 21 + 12) / 4.
4. Debrief: when DOES adding a value raise the mean? Have the group write the rule (above the mean raises it, below lowers it, equal keeps it).

content.worked_problem: Data: 15, 18, 21 (mean 18). A new value of 12 is added. Noah says: 'Adding a value makes the data set bigger, so the mean must increase.'
content.error_step: Noah assumed more data means a higher mean, without comparing the new value to the current mean.
content.why: The sum grows by 12 but the divisor grows too: (15 + 18 + 21 + 12) / 4 = 66 / 4 = 16.5. A value below the old mean of 18 pulls the mean DOWN.

activities.title: See-Saw the Mean
activities.instructions:
1. Tape values 0-12 along a ruler and balance it on a pencil at the mean of a small data set (e.g. coins at 4, 6, 8 balance at 6).
2. Ask: where will the ruler tip if I add a coin at 12? At 2? Right at 6?
3. Add the coin and watch. Reconnect: the balance point IS the mean, and a new value tips it toward itself.
4. Debrief: why does a coin placed exactly at the balance point change nothing?

activities.title: Predict, Then Prove
activities.instructions:
1. Write a 4-value data set on the board and compute its mean as a class.
2. Partner A draws a number card -- that value joins the data.
3. BOTH partners secretly write a prediction: mean up, down, or same? Median up, down, or same?
4. Compute together. Each correct prediction earns a point; a correct prediction WITH a because-sentence earns two.
5. Rotate. After 4 rounds, ask: what's the fastest way to predict the mean's direction?

strategy_links.why: Noah's 'bigger data, bigger mean' claim is a crisp, testable error -- disproving it by computation rewrites the rule.
The balanced-ruler model makes 'above pulls up, below pulls down' a physical fact before it's an abstract rule.
Gradual release fits the predict-then-verify routine: model it, predict together, then students predict and prove alone.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, the interquartile range from a box plot, which forces ordering, medians, and display reading all at once. If they pass, check the interpretive skills S5 (shape and choosing a measure) and S6 (predicting change). If they fail, drop one grade below to the B skills: B1 checks reading and building a line plot, and B2 checks the mean, median, and range of a whole-number set, the grade five statistics 6.DS.3 is built on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (multi-digit addition and subtraction) and F2 (whole-number division) locate the arithmetic gap in grades 3 and 4. S1, S2, and S3 stay available to probe the standard's own median, mean, and display-reading work.
